messages.author: ebb379a3a0fffc45
messages.subject: Moderated Regressions vs. SEM, how to choose?
parts:
Dear all,


I’m trying to run this model in R (figure below) but hesitate on the approach to adopt:


I can run a Moderated Multiple Regressions, if I’m correct, with model under R like this:


model <- ‘ DV1<-lm(DV1~IV*Student+IV*Married+IV*Income)

    DV2<-lm(DV2~IV*Age+IV*Sex)’

Summary (model)


But since some of the variables are categorical (like the IV, the student and Sex) while others are somehow continuous (Income, Age, etc… the 2 DVs have a Poisson distribution though), isn’t it more practical to use the Lavaan package here even though all my variables are observed?


Thanks a lot for your insights!


Jordane

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Moderated Regressions vs. SEM, how to choose?
parts: One precision, I would still need to do only on model with 2 separate regressions in it?
No, it is one regression model to predict one DV.  And another regression model to predict another DV.

Like this?

ModelDV1 <- glm(DV1~IV*Student+IV*Married+IV*Income, family=poisson(link=log), data=DF)
Correct
But how do I insert the second regression in the same model?

What?  You seem to be over-interpreting your path diagram.  Arrows pointing to arrows is a conceptual depiction of moderation that does not conform to the statistical model you would actually fit.  You should read an introductory regression textbook to learn about statistical interactions, which estimate moderating effects using product terms.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

If you have clustered data, you also need to read a book about multilevel modeling, and use software for that (e.g., the glmer() function in the lme4 package).

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Moderated Regressions vs. SEM, how to choose?
parts: The thing is the data are indeed clustered, but my model does not have prediction in the second level (state). I'm looking for a way to control for the clustering effect without going for a multi-level approach (which make sense to me only in case of 2nd level prediction), right? Is there a way to control this on R?

You are not required to have hypotheses about 2nd-level effects to use multilevel modeling.  But you can also fit a marginal model using generalized estimating equations.  See the gee or geepack packages, for example.  There might be others.  Try asking on Cross Validated, which is more general than this site (devoted to lavaan questions, which are no longer what you are asking).

https://stats.stackexchange.com/

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
